title: Renewed Interest in Teeth Whitening After Years of Mask-Wearing
excerpt: Discover why many Londoners are exploring teeth whitening after years of mask-wearing, and what to consider before starting treatment.
author: Teeth Whitening Team
imageAlt: Renewed Interest in Teeth Whitening After Years of Mask-Wearing
body:
Introduction

Many people across London are noticing their smiles more consciously than they have in years. After an extended period during which face masks were part of daily life — covering mouths and reducing the visibility of teeth in social, professional, and public settings — interest in teeth whitening has seen a meaningful resurgence. For many adults, the return to mask-free environments has brought fresh attention to the appearance of their teeth, especially in video-first professional settings.

If you have found yourself wondering whether your teeth look different than you remembered, or whether whitening treatment might be right for you, you are not alone. Searching online for teeth whitening information is completely understandable, and doing your research before seeking professional advice is a sensible first step.

This article explains the background to renewed interest in whitening treatments, what causes tooth discolouration, how professional whitening works, and what to consider before pursuing any treatment. It also explains when a clinical assessment with a qualified dental professional would be a helpful next step.

What Is Teeth Whitening and Is It Right for You After Mask-Wearing?

Teeth whitening is a cosmetic dental procedure that uses clinically approved bleaching agents to lighten the natural shade of tooth enamel. Following years during which face masks reduced daily awareness of smile appearance, many adults are now revisiting their dental aesthetics. Suitability for teeth whitening depends on individual dental health and requires a clinical assessment from a registered dental professional.

Why Has Interest in Teeth Whitening Increased?

It is hardly surprising that many people have taken a closer look at their smiles since face coverings became less prevalent in everyday life. During periods of widespread mask use, the visible portion of the face shifted primarily to the eyes. Social interactions, video calls, and public appearances all took place with mouths largely concealed, meaning many individuals paid less conscious attention to the appearance of their teeth.

As mask-wearing has reduced, people are once again engaging face-to-face without facial coverings — at work, social occasions, and in photographs. For some, this renewed visibility has prompted a reassessment of how their smile looks and feels.

At the same time, it is worth noting that this shift in attention does not necessarily mean teeth have changed significantly during this period. Rather, it may reflect a renewed awareness of something that was temporarily out of mind. That said, natural tooth discolouration is a gradual and common process, and it is entirely reasonable to want to understand your options.

Importantly, any decision regarding cosmetic dental treatment should begin with a professional consultation, as suitability varies from person to person.

What Causes Tooth Discolouration?

Understanding why teeth change colour is an important starting point before exploring any whitening treatment. Tooth discolouration can be grouped into two main categories: extrinsic and intrinsic staining.

Extrinsic staining occurs on the outer surface of teeth — the enamel — and is typically caused by:

  • Regular consumption of tea, coffee, and red wine
  • Tobacco use (smoking or chewing)
  • Certain foods with strong pigments, such as berries or curry
  • Poor oral hygiene over time

Intrinsic staining occurs within the inner structure of the tooth, known as dentine, and can be caused by:

  • Certain medications taken during tooth development (such as tetracycline antibiotics)
  • Excessive fluoride exposure during childhood (dental fluorosis)
  • Trauma to a tooth
  • Natural ageing, which causes dentine to darken and enamel to thin

Understanding which type of discolouration is present is clinically important, because not all staining responds equally to whitening treatments. A dental professional can assess this during a consultation and recommend an appropriate approach, if suitable.

How Does Professional Teeth Whitening Work?

Professional teeth whitening uses peroxide-based bleaching agents — typically hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide — to penetrate tooth enamel and break down pigmented molecules within the tooth structure. This results in a lightening of the tooth's overall shade.

In the United Kingdom, dental whitening products containing more than 0.1% hydrogen peroxide may only be legally administered or supplied by a regulated dental professional. This is an important distinction, as it separates clinically appropriate treatment from many over-the-counter or beauty-salon products that may not be regulated to the same standard.

Professional teeth whitening is generally offered in two main formats:

  • In-surgery whitening: A higher-concentration gel is applied to the teeth under controlled clinical conditions, often with a light or laser to activate the bleaching agent. Results may be seen in a single session.
  • Take-home whitening trays: Custom-fitted trays are made to fit your teeth precisely, and a lower-concentration gel is provided to use at home over a prescribed period.

Both approaches can be effective when clinically appropriate. Results vary depending on the original shade of the teeth, the cause of discolouration, and individual dental health factors. A dental professional can advise on which option may be most suitable following a thorough examination.

You can learn more about the professional whitening options available by visiting the teeth whitening treatments page at our London practice.

The Science Behind Tooth Enamel and Whitening

To understand how whitening works — and why it may not be suitable for everyone — it helps to understand a little about tooth anatomy.

Each tooth is made up of several layers. The outermost visible layer is enamel, a hard, semi-translucent mineralised tissue. Beneath it lies dentine, a yellower layer that gives teeth much of their natural colour. As we age, enamel gradually thins through a combination of dietary acid exposure, mechanical wear, and natural ageing. This makes the darker dentine beneath more visible, contributing to a yellower appearance over time.

Whitening agents work primarily within the enamel layer and the outer surface of dentine, breaking apart the chemical bonds of stain molecules. However, whitening does not change the colour of dental restorations such as crowns, veneers, or composite bonding — an important consideration for anyone who has existing dental work on visible teeth.

Additionally, whitening is not appropriate for teeth with active decay, gum disease, or significant sensitivity issues. This is why a clinical examination prior to any treatment is essential. Attempting whitening without addressing underlying dental health issues could cause discomfort or be clinically counterproductive.

Is Teeth Whitening Suitable for Everyone?

Teeth whitening is a widely used cosmetic dental treatment, but it is not universally appropriate. Suitability depends on a range of clinical and personal factors that a dental professional is best placed to assess.

Whitening may not be recommended in cases where:

  • Active tooth decay or gum disease is present (this should be treated first)
  • Teeth have significant sensitivity or exposed root surfaces
  • The patient is pregnant or breastfeeding
  • The patient is under 18 years of age (whitening is not recommended for younger patients)
  • The primary discolouration is intrinsic and unlikely to respond to bleaching
  • Existing dental restorations are present on prominent front teeth, as these will not change shade

Even where whitening is appropriate, results differ between individuals. It is not possible to predict a precise outcome without clinical assessment, and responsible dental communication should never guarantee specific results. The aim is always to support individual patients in making informed decisions that are right for their oral health and personal circumstances.

If you are considering professional whitening, booking a cosmetic dental consultation is a sensible first step to understand what may be achievable for you.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

If you are noticing changes to the appearance of your teeth, or if you are experiencing any of the following alongside cosmetic concerns, it may be worth arranging a dental appointment:

  • Tooth sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweet foods and drinks, which can indicate enamel thinning or exposed dentine
  • Visible changes in tooth colour that seem sudden or affect only one tooth, which may point to internal issues such as trauma or pulp changes
  • Gum recession or soreness, which may affect whether whitening is appropriate
  • It has been more than a year since your last dental check-up, as a routine examination is recommended regardless of cosmetic interest
  • You have existing dental restorations and want to understand how whitening would interact with these

None of these situations require alarm, but each warrants a calm and professional review. A dental check-up allows your dentist to assess your overall oral health and discuss any cosmetic options that may be appropriate for you.

Maintaining Oral Health and Reducing Discolouration Over Time

Regardless of whether teeth whitening is something you choose to pursue, there are practical steps that can help maintain the natural brightness of your teeth and support good long-term oral health.

Diet and lifestyle habits:

  • Reduce consumption of teeth-staining drinks such as coffee, tea, and red wine, or rinse your mouth with water after consuming them
  • Avoid or reduce tobacco use, which is one of the most significant contributors to extrinsic staining
  • Use a straw when drinking acidic or pigmented beverages to limit contact with enamel

Daily oral hygiene:

  • Brush teeth thoroughly twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste
  • Floss or use interdental brushes daily to remove plaque from between teeth
  • Consider an electric toothbrush, which some clinical evidence suggests may assist in removing surface staining compared to manual brushing for some individuals.

Professional care:

  • Attend regular dental check-ups, typically every six to twelve months as advised by your dentist
  • Professional hygiene appointments (scale and polish) can remove surface staining that home brushing cannot

Good oral health is the foundation upon which any cosmetic dental treatment is built. Maintaining healthy gums and enamel gives you the best starting point for any future whitening or cosmetic treatment.

You may also find it helpful to explore professional hygiene and stain removal services as part of maintaining a healthy smile.

Key Points to Remember

  • Renewed awareness of smile appearance after years of mask-wearing is a completely understandable and common experience among adults in London.
  • Teeth whitening is a clinically regulated procedure in the UK — only qualified dental professionals can legally provide treatments above 0.1% hydrogen peroxide.
  • Not everyone is a suitable candidate for whitening; clinical assessment is required to determine suitability.
  • Discolouration has different causes — extrinsic staining responds differently to whitening compared with intrinsic discolouration.
  • Existing dental restorations such as crowns, veneers, and composite bonding will not change shade with whitening treatment.
  • Good oral hygiene and regular dental appointments form the essential foundation for both dental health and cosmetic treatment outcomes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is teeth whitening safe?

Professional teeth whitening, when carried out by a qualified and GDC-registered dental professional using regulated products, is considered a safe procedure for suitable patients. As with any clinical treatment, there can be side effects, with temporary tooth sensitivity being the most commonly reported. A thorough dental examination before treatment helps to identify any factors that might increase sensitivity or make whitening unsuitable, allowing your dentist to advise you appropriately before you proceed.

How long do teeth whitening results typically last?

The longevity of whitening results varies considerably between individuals and depends on factors including diet, lifestyle habits, and natural tooth characteristics. Results can typically last anywhere from several months to a couple of years. Avoiding or reducing staining foods and drinks, maintaining good oral hygiene, and attending regular dental appointments can all help to preserve results. Some patients choose to use top-up home whitening trays periodically, under dental guidance, to maintain their shade.

Can teeth whitening damage enamel?

When carried out using clinically appropriate products at recommended concentrations, professional teeth whitening is not considered to cause lasting enamel damage. Temporary sensitivity during or after treatment is a recognised and usually short-lived effect. Using unregulated products purchased from non-dental sources — such as beauty salons or online retailers — carries a higher risk of misuse and may be associated with greater risk of sensitivity or soft tissue irritation. This is one reason why professional supervision matters.

Why won't teeth whitening work on my dental crowns or veneers?

Whitening agents work by penetrating the natural enamel structure to break down organic stain molecules. Dental restorations such as porcelain crowns, ceramic veneers, and composite bonding are fabricated from materials that do not contain the same organic structures as natural enamel. As a result, bleaching agents have no lightening effect on these restorations. If you have visible restorations on your front teeth and wish to whiten, your dental team can advise on the most appropriate way to approach this, which may include considering replacement of any restorations after whitening.

Do I need to see a dentist before whitening, even if I buy an at-home kit?

In the UK, legally compliant at-home whitening trays supplied above the threshold concentration should only be provided by a dental professional following a clinical assessment. This consultation ensures your teeth and gums are healthy enough for treatment and that custom-fitted trays are created to minimise gel contact with gum tissue. Purchasing whitening products directly from retailers without dental oversight carries clinical and legal risks. It is always advisable to seek professional guidance before beginning any whitening treatment.

What is the difference between whitening toothpaste and professional teeth whitening?

Whitening toothpastes typically work through mild abrasive ingredients that help to remove surface staining during brushing, or through low-level chemical agents. They can be useful for maintaining surface cleanliness but do not contain the peroxide concentrations used in professional whitening and therefore cannot achieve the same degree of shade change. Professional whitening treatment targets deeper pigmentation within the enamel and dentine, producing more significant results. Your dentist can help you understand which approach — or combination of approaches — may be most appropriate for your situation.

Conclusion

Renewed interest in teeth whitening following years of mask-wearing is a completely natural response to re-engaging with mask-free social and professional life. Many adults across London are now thinking carefully about their smile for the first time in a while, and seeking information is an entirely sensible starting point.

Teeth whitening is considered a clinically appropriate and well-tolerated cosmetic treatment for suitable patients when provided by a qualified dental professional using regulated products. However, it is not universally appropriate, and individual suitability depends on factors including existing dental health, the nature of any discolouration, and the presence of dental restorations.

If you are considering whitening treatment, the most important first step is a professional dental consultation. This allows your dentist to assess your oral health, discuss what whitening may and may not achieve, and help you make an informed, confident decision.

Maintaining good oral hygiene, attending regular check-ups, and making mindful lifestyle choices remain the most reliable ways to support a healthy and bright smile over the long term.
